documents.abstract: Arthritis is one of the leading causes of chronic pain, disability, and reduced quality of life worldwide, affecting millions of individuals through progressive joint inflammation, cartilage degeneration, and bone destruction.Although conventional therapies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologics, and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, effectively alleviate symptoms and delay disease progression, their long-term use is frequently associated with adverse effects, high treatment costs, and incomplete disease remission.Consequently, phytotherapy has emerged as a promising complementary and alternative therapeutic strategy owing to its multitarget pharmacological actions and comparatively favorable safety profile.This review comprehensively summarizes the current knowledge on the pathophysiology of arthritis, emphasizing inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and major intracellular signaling pathways, including NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, PI3K/Akt, NLRP3 inflammasome, COX-2, and 5-lipoxygenase.Particular attention is given to bioactive phytoconstituents such as curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin, kaempferol, luteolin, apigenin, catechins, boswellic acids, thymoquinone, berberine, and other polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, saponins, tannins, and glycosides.Furthermore, the review compiles experimental pharmacological evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies, summarizes medicinal plants with established anti-arthritic activity, and highlights their molecular targets and mechanisms of action.Emerging advances in nanotechnology-based phytopharmaceuticals, molecular docking, network pharmacology, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence are also discussed as future directions for improving the efficacy, bioavailability, and precision of plant-derived therapeutics.Collectively, the available evidence indicates that phytochemicals exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and chondroprotective effects through simultaneous modulation of multiple molecular pathways.However, further standardization, pharmacokinetic evaluation, and well-designed multicenter clinical trials are required to facilitate their successful translation into evidence-based clinical practice.This review provides an integrated scientific framework for researchers and clinicians involved in the development of safer, multitarget, and effective phytotherapeutic interventions for arthritis management.

The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, offer a global guide to eliminate poverty, safeguard the planet, and promote prosperity by 2030. Higher education institutions (HEIs) are uniquely well placed as a knowledge centre to hasten the pace of learning by performing their main roles, such as academia (teaching and learning), administration (governance and operation), and innovation and research. The current study aims to find ways Artificial Intelligence (AI) can boost sustainability and what challenges and chances it brings in managing and promoting sustainability. The results show that AI can optimize resources by using models that predict how to cut down on energy use, improve how people move around campus, and reduce waste. In teaching, AI makes things more sustainable by offering personalized learning, digital tutoring, instant feedback, and immersive experiences to enhance student motivation and engagement. In research, AI can make a significant impact by making it easier to analyze big datasets on environmental, social, and economic topics. The study finds that responsible and fair AI implementation in academia, administration, and research is necessary to help HEIs close SDG gaps. Three major recommendations are: ethical AI governance and faculty development, AI-optimized sustainable campus operation, and interdisciplinary AI-driven research hubs. In recent years, the demand for strategic adoption of AI in higher education has increased, particularly to fulfill SDGs and ensure that all people enjoy peace and prosperity by 2030. This study encourages institutions to establish funded AI hubs that foster cross-disciplinary research and international collaborations to produce evidence-based solutions to various SDGs, such as health (SDG 3), clean energy (SDG 7), and biodiversity (SDG 15).

Purpose This study aims to explore how personalized services provided by pre-consultation chatbots influence patients' intentions to self-disclose and the boundary conditions of this effect. Drawing on the Communication Privacy Management Theory, it identifies AI interactive trust as a mediator and examines how disease sensitivity moderates this mechanism. Design/methodology/approach Three scenario experiments and a field survey were conducted to test hypotheses. Experiments 1 and 2 were between-subjects experiments that manipulated pre-consultation chatbot service personalization (low vs. high) in different disease contexts. Experiment 3 employed a 2 (service personalization: low vs. high) × 2 (disease type: low- vs. high-sensitivity) between-subjects design. Survey 4 reconfirmed all hypotheses. Findings Service personalization increased patients' willingness to self-disclose by enhancing AI interactive trust, but only for low-sensitivity diseases. For high-sensitivity conditions, this trust-based effect weakens or even disappears. Originality/value By uncovering the central role of relationship quality in human-AI interactions, this study delivers novel theoretical insights, distinct from prior benefit-risk frameworks, into the internal mechanisms by which AI service personalization shapes users' willingness to self-disclose, extending existing research on the mechanisms of personalized AI services.

documents.abstract: Intelligent Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) has a pivotal place in sarcasm detection, given that sarcastic utterances may have an intended meaning that is not in the literal meaning of the spoken words. Sarcasm is also difficult to spot correctly since it varies not only in text but also in voice and other visual indicators like facial expression and body language. Unimodal sarcasm detection methods are generally limited by contextual ambiguity, the insensitivity of contextual paralinguistic cues, and decreased performance in situations where one modality is noisy or incomplete. These problems may cause unpredictable results and inadequate functionality in the real conversational context. To overcome these shortcomings, for sarcasm detection, we suggest an approach with different modalities which uses multi-modal cues like audio, video as well as text to provide complementary information from various communication channels. In the case of textual representation, the RoBERTa architecture was used to elicit deep contextual and semantic features of dialog transcripts. The HuBERT architecture was used to model acoustic features and is effective at representing speech representations in terms of prosodic and tonal variation based on sarcastic speech. Simultaneously, the ViViT architecture was used to process visual data and identify both spatial and temporal patterns of facial expressions and gestures in videos. Modality-specific feature representations are then combined with a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) based fusion strategy which decides best-found modality weights by minimizing classification loss. The fused representation is then optimized and then through the two-layer fully connected classifier to classify sarcasm. The suggested framework was evaluated with the publicly available MUStARD dataset. The model displayed an accuracy of 94% and the recall, precision and weighted F1-score were all equal to 0.94. Comparative evaluation also compared the proposed PSO-Multimodal Fusion Model with the unimodal models and also with the traditional multimodal fusion models such as attention-based model, Graph-based model, Generative Approach, LLM/Modeling-based model, and contrastive learning approach, and showed that the proposed multimodal fusion framework yields the highest weighted F1-score among the evaluated approaches. Experimental outcomes prove that the multimodal fusion methodology based on optimization enhances the performance of sarcasm detection in contrast to the unimodal and traditional fusion techniques, which indicate its efficiency in practical use in conversational AI.

Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) in commercial aviation raise critical safety challenges in complex, time-pressured situations where human expertise is paramount. This study investigates how AI-based Human-Autonomy Teaming (HAT) can support pilot decision-making under high workload, compromised situational awareness, and time pressure. In a high-fidelity Airbus A320 simulator, 22 airline pilots performed a fuel- and time-constrained approach scenario designed to challenge HAT’s operational effectiveness under four conditions: no assistance, on-demand AI, proactive AI, and proactive explainable AI. Workload (NASA-TLX) remained high across conditions, yet decision-making differed markedly. Without assistance, only 20% chose the safest landing option; with on-demand AI, 40%; and with proactive AI (both versions), 100%. Explainable AI yielded the highest scenario comprehension (75%), matching two-crew baseline performance. Proactive systems increased decision and SA related interactions, fostering a collaborative dynamic akin to traditional crew resource management. Thus, the results demonstrate that, in the context of SPO, proactive and explainable AI was associated with crew-level decision performance within the experimental scenario without adding cognitive load. Beyond the aeronautical domain, our results are of interest for the design of cognitive support systems for high-risk domains where teams composed of humans and AI must adapt in real time.

Teachers' limited competence in utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based digital media has hindered the effective implementation of innovative teaching practices and environmental projects. This community service program aimed to enhance teachers' knowledge and skills in developing AI-based instructional media. The program was conducted at State Senior High School 1 Koto Kampar Hulu and involved 29 teachers through educational seminars, workshops, hands-on practice, and mentoring using Canva AI, Gemini AI, and NotebookLM. Program effectiveness was evaluated using pretest-posttest assessments, N-Gain analysis, instructional media product evaluation, and participant satisfaction questionnaires. The results showed that the participants' mean score increased from 47.0 to 78.9, with an N-Gain score of 0.6, indicating a moderate level of improvement. All participants (100%) demonstrated increased knowledge following the training. Furthermore, every participant successfully developed at least one AI-based instructional medium, such as a poster or infographic, that was ready for implementation in classroom instruction and environmental projects. These findings indicate that the training effectively enhanced teachers' digital competencies and their ability to integrate AI technologies into teaching and learning practices

documents.abstract: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Technical, social, avant-garde, global, and cognitive pressures are driving the adoption of new technologies characterized by constant updates and automation most notably generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents. While the stated intention is to augment and enhance human capabilities regarding complex challenges, skills, and critical thinking rather than replacing them recent empirical evidence suggests the actual trend is moving in the opposite direction, to the detriment of consumers. This study analyzes the flaws and risks stemming from the use and misuse of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose intervention frameworks before they become irreversibly entrenched in a fragile structure within the technology adoption cycle. It explores phenomena such as the atrophy of technical skills, the productivity paradox, cognitive offloading, over-reliance on automated systems, and the irony of automation, drawing on evidence from randomized controlled trials and large-scale surveys conducted between 2025 and 2026. This analysis examines the critical failures and systemic risks of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose regulatory and operational intervention frameworks before their negative effects become irreversibly embedded in the labor market and social fabric. Identifying these risk vectors early allows for the design of guidelines that restore human control, ensuring technology acts as a genuine complement rather than an agent of cognitive and professional erosion. Furthermore, there is high demand for courses, diploma programs, and workshops focused on critical thinking, reflecting a growing awareness of the need to pursue them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas became the first papal encyclical on artificial intelligence, declaring that lethal decisions cannot be entrusted to artificial systems and calling for a shared international framework to govern military AI. It states these principles but does not operationalise them. This article develops that operational framework. Applying Catholic social doctrine (human dignity and agency, subsidiarity, prudence, intentionality, the common good, and the protection of noncombatants) to military AI, it translates the encyclical's commitments into concrete requirements for autonomous weapons, targeting systems, and alliance interoperability. It grounds the argument in the nuclear precedent, where Catholic ethics shaped doctrine as it formed, and more briefly in chemical and biological weapons prohibition. Engaging just war theory, NATO's Principles of Responsible Use, recent military wargaming, and a leading AI provider's treatment of a catastrophic strike as consistent with its self-declared “red lines,” it shows where Catholic ethics is more demanding than procedural compliance. It then proposes institutional mechanisms: a tiered deliberation framework, proportionality dossiers, ethics review boards, and NATO-level coordination. Building ethical architecture before deployment, the article argues, serves strategic as well as moral interests.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Ethnic diversity significantly influences anaesthetic pharmacology and perioperative outcomes through complex interactions between genetic, physiological, environmental and social determinants of health. There is increasing evidence suggesting that different ethnic populations demonstrate variability in anaesthetic drug metabolism, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pain perception and recovery characteristics. Pharmacogenomic variations in cytochrome P450 enzymes contribute to clinically significant differences in opioid metabolism, sedative and analgesic response, and postoperative recovery. In addition, epigenetic influences, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, may further affect pain modulation, opioid responsiveness and susceptibility to perioperative neurocognitive effects. Ethnic disparities in perioperative care extend beyond biological variability, with minority populations demonstrating differences in access to regional anaesthesia, obstetric anaesthesia services, perioperative pain management and paediatric perioperative care. Various factors, like structural inequalities, communication barriers, implicit bias and unequal healthcare, contribute to these disparities. Advances in pharmacogenomics, artificial intelligence and precision perioperative medicine may lead to more individualized anaesthetic management in the future. However, important challenges, such as limited representation of diverse populations in research, and limited understanding of gene – environment interactions, need to be addressed. A better understanding of ethnic variability in anaesthetic pharmacology may improve anaesthetic safety, optimize perioperative drug dosing and selection, and promote equitable perioperative care across diverse patient populations.

Background Nail technicians face significant risks of musculoskeletal disorders due to ergonomic challenges. Nail technicians’ working conditions and health risks can be evaluated to develop strategies that enhance their well-being. Objective This study assesses the working conditions, occupational symptoms, and potential risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders among nail technicians. Methods This cross-sectional study involved 35 female nail technicians. Data were collected through interviews, pain assessments, occupational details, the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire, and the Quick Exposure Check (QEC) for ergonomic risks. Results A significant proportion of technicians reported respiratory issues (37.1%), skin problems (14.2%), and musculoskeletal pain, particularly in the neck (51%), upper back (57%), and lower back (31%). QEC levels showed that back static positions and neck and wrist/hand exposures were in the “very high risk” category, while shoulder/arm exposures were classified as “high risk”. Neck and static back QEC scores were significantly correlated with weekly working hours and years of experience (r = 0.828, p < 0.001), and reported pain was strongly linked to QEC risk scores for these areas (r = 0.944, p < 0.001). Conclusions The findings regarding nail technicians’ working conditions and health risks underscore the necessity for ergonomic training and workplace modifications to mitigate these risks. Early intervention is essential to prevent chronic work-related disorders and improve technicians’ health and quality of life.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.

documents.abstract: EVIE-STREAM develops a mathematical and computational framework for learning clean behavioral response probabilities from corrupted, fragmented, and delayed records. Its central advance is an explicit five-event mechanism that separates asymmetric recording errors from heterogeneous underlying behavior, together with a matching impossibility result, statistical learning limits, and an executed neural behavioral-cloning implementation. The research addresses a fundamental ambiguity in personalized AI: an observed response distribution can reflect both a person’s preferences and the errors introduced by the recording process. Increasing model capacity or collecting more observations through the same unidentified channel does not necessarily resolve that ambiguity. EVIE-STREAM identifies additional observable relationships that can make clean behavioral learning possible. 1. An explicit five-event identification mechanism The principal mathematical result concerns a binary capture channel with independently occurring, potentially unequal false-positive and false-negative rates. Each calibration donor may have a different unknown behavioral prevalence and Markov persistence, while sharing the recording channel within a source. For five consecutive observations, the manuscript derives an observable quadratic whose two roots recover the channel parameters. Every valid nondegenerate stationary donor contributes an identification signal with the same sign. Consequently, arbitrary heterogeneity in donor prevalence and persistence cannot cancel the aggregate signal. This permits calibration without clean donor labels, knowledge of individual donor parameters, or a requirement that donors behave like the target person. Donor records estimate the recording mechanism; the target’s own attributed records determine the personal behavioral policy. 2. A sharp four-to-five observation boundary The release supplies an exact four-event nonidentifiability construction: two different asymmetric channels, combined with different positive donor mixtures, produce the same complete observed four-event distribution. Together with the five-event identity, this establishes a sharp local-window threshold for the declared observation class: one independent, consecutive window per anonymous, arbitrarily heterogeneous stationary Markov donor. The distinction has a concrete acquisition consequence. Preserving a fifth valid consecutive event can supply an identifying relationship that arbitrarily many unrelated four-event windows fail to provide. Reliable estimation still requires many independent windows. Other observation designs, including linked repeated windows from known donors, can have different thresholds. 3. Matching information limits for calibration and clean learning The manuscript establishes matching upper and lower bounds for channel estimation and finite-context behavioral learning. Its effective donor information budget is [I_D=\sum_j m_j\kappa_j^4,] where (m_j) counts independent calibration windows and (\kappa_j) is a declared persistence lower bound. Under the stated compact nondegeneracy assumptions, channel endpoint mean-squared error has order [\frac{1}{1+I_D}.] For (d) balanced known contexts and (N) independent noisy target labels, clean-policy estimation risk has order [\min\left{1,\frac{d}{N}+\frac{1}{1+I_D}\right}.] These results separate two unavoidable information requirements: learning the target’s behavior and identifying the process that corrupts its observations. They also explain why additional target records can eventually provide diminishing benefit when calibration uncertainty remains unresolved. 4. A working connection to neural AI training EVIE-STREAM implements a neural policy that predicts clean action probabilities and trains through a calibrated, source-specific observation layer: \widehat a_s+(\widehat b_s-\widehat a_s)q_\phi(x,i).] Here, (q_\phi) represents the clean behavioral policy, while the fitted channel predicts how that behavior would appear in the recorded data. Deployment uses the clean policy directly. The release derives an exact soft-posterior training gradient and an architecture-independent inequality connecting clean behavioral error to population observation-likelihood error and channel-estimation error. This provides a mathematical connection between calibration quality and neural prediction fidelity. 5. Executed experiments with 192 trained neural policies The release contains 192 trained neural policies across two synthetic studies using 16 paired seeds. Each policy has 1,105 parameters and learns context-dependent binary behavior for four simulated identities. In the primary study, source-specific asymmetric calibration reduced expected excess clean log loss by 56.38% relative to naive noisy-label training. It tied the simpler symmetric correction under equal source exposure. A subsequent explanatory stress protocol, fixed before stress training, changed source exposure to 85/15 while reusing the underlying records and calibration captures. In this setting, the original asymmetric method achieved: 47.16% lower excess clean log loss than symmetric correction. 62.25% lower excess clean log loss than naive training. Improvement over symmetric correction in all 16 paired seeds. A 1.121 percentage-point increase in modal-action accuracy over symmetric correction. The stress study shares records and seeds with the primary study and is not an independent replication. The release retains the primary tie, secondary refinements, oracle comparisons, acquisition costs, and context-shift results. Saved-model audits reproduce 3,145,728 stored predictions across all 192 models, with zero reload discrepancy in the recorded runtime. 6. Acquisition principles and long-term consistency The theory yields an acquisition principle beyond simply collecting longer or more repetitive records. For positive donor persistence, the calibration signal contains the factor (\rho^2(1-\rho)), which is maximized at (\rho=2/3). Nearly independent and nearly frozen behavior both provide weak signal through this mechanism. The framework also includes confidence-set procedures, source-prioritization heuristics, persistent-reference update guards, and conditional bounds connecting one-step policy error to finite-horizon trajectory differences. These mechanisms make calibration uncertainty, context coverage, and accumulated behavioral drift explicit. What is distinctive and potentially important The proposed new contribution is the combination of an explicit heterogeneous-donor quintet identity, an exact shorter-window obstruction, matching information limits, and an executed calibration-to-neural-learning pipeline. The work builds on established hidden Markov identification and forward loss correction; its contribution concerns the particular observation class, algebraic mechanism, and resulting learning guarantees. Potential applications include source calibration for behavioral-cloning systems, AI agents learning binary decisions from noisy event logs, and personalized decision models assembled from fragmented histories. Where the assumptions can be validated, the method offers a way to recover information about behavior without absorbing source-specific recording bias into the learned policy. Scope and reproducibility The temporal theory assumes stationary homogeneous binary Markov behavior within valid windows, intact local chronology, conditionally independent memoryless capture errors, and a shared oriented channel within each source. Quantitative guarantees require additional nondegeneracy conditions. Delayed records are evaluated through a fixed availability deadline in the neural experiments. All experimental records are synthetic. No human digital clone, transformer, conversational language model, or speech system was trained or evaluated. Human behavioral fidelity and unconditional lifelong identity preservation remain future research objectives. Scientific priority remains unestablished. The release includes the 27-page manuscript, complete proofs, exact certificates, raw main-study synthetic captures, trained weights, experimental protocols, inference interfaces, reproduction scripts, internal audits, and preserved earlier research. documents.abstract: The article examines the evolution of UX/UI design tools in the context of the rapid development of the contemporary digital environment. The principal stages in the transformation of digital interface design tools are considered, from traditional graphic editors and static layouts to specialised UX/UI platforms, interactive prototyping, cloud-based environments, component-based design, and design systems. The impact of digital technologies on the organisation of UX/UI design processes is analysed, including the spread of collaborative tools, the integration of design into software development workflows, and the automation of individual design stages. Particular attention is paid to the current phase of UX/UI tool development associated with artificial intelligence, generative design, and AI-assisted workflows. The main trends in the further development of UX/UI design tools and the transformation of the designer’s professional role are identified. It is argued that digital design tools are evolving towards the integration of design, prototyping, user research, software development, and artificial intelligence within a unified environment aimed at creating effective, accessible, and personalised user experiences.

Predictive toxicology is vital for drug safety and human health protection, yet traditional toxicological methods are limited by cost, time, ethical issues, and poor human relevance. New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including in vitro, in silico, and in chemico techniques, offer mechanism-based and human-relevant alternatives. Advances in artificial intelligence have enhanced toxicity prediction from complex datasets, but limited interpretability has restricted regulatory acceptance. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) improves transparency and trust by revealing the biological and chemical drivers behind model decisions. This chapter per the authors examines the integration of XAI with NAMs as an advanced framework for predictive toxicology, highlighting its applications in toxicity prediction, dose–response assessment, and early safety evaluation, while addressing challenges related to data quality, validation, and standardization.

ABSTRACT Big data analytics plays a crucial role in providing usable insights for improving the strategic planning of the diagnosis methods in the healthcare industry, and here the big data helps the clinical professionals analyze the large numbers of datasets obtained from different demographic groups to identify which factor is blocking the patients from taking up their treatment. Despite the benefits guided by the information age, healthcare technologies encounter difficulties such as data protection, loss, and management issues. Artificial intelligence (AI) has helped more in the adaptation and handled the pandemic situations. However, the realization of AI's potential in healthcare is tempered by concerns regarding the trustworthiness and explaining ability of AI systems. ML algorithms have shown promise in detecting and managing healthcare complications, while the deployment of critical medical Internet of Things applications necessitates efficient mechanisms to address patient privacy concerns. Furthermore, the use of AI and machine learning (ML) in healthcare enables disease outbreak prediction, highlighting the versatility of AI in the health sector. However, there are still obstacles to achieving interpretability and accuracy in AI systems. Given these challenges, explainable AI (XAI) methods that are technically capable, ethically responsible, and meet the needs of healthcare practitioners are increasingly important. This review sky‐scrapes the importance of transparency, effective data management, human oversight, and international collaboration in advancing XAI in healthcare. Ultimately, the paper calls for the generalization of XAI frameworks and the prioritization of interpretation, data privacy, and security for future research, which has the full potential of XAI in revolutionizing healthcare.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed pharmacology and toxicology by enabling high-dimensional pattern recognition across chemical, biological, and clinical datasets. However, the dominance of opaque “black-box” models has limited their adoption in mechanistic toxicology and regulatory-grade safety assessment, where scientific interpretability, causal reasoning, and traceable evidence are mandatory. This chapter explores the paradigm shift from predictive but inscrutable AI systems toward explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) frameworks that provide biologically meaningful, mechanistically grounded, and regulator-trustworthy insights. We review the historical evolution of computational toxicology, outline core concepts in explainability, and map XAI methods to toxicological use cases spanning molecular initiating events, adverse outcome pathways, organ-level toxicity, and population-level risk assessment.

Machine learning models are now widely used to forecast stock price movements and to measure financial risk, yet most cannot explain their own outputs. In finance that is a serious weakness, because forecasts influence real investment decisions and regulators expect firms to justify the models they use. This review asks how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been applied to stock trend prediction and risk as-sessment, and how far the resulting explanations can be trusted. We first outline the economic theory of predictability and the standard risk measures, then set out the mathematics of the main explanation methods: Shapley-value attribution, LIME, gradient-based attribution, attention, and counterfactuals. We then compare representative studies, summarise regulatory expectations, and propose a five-layer framework for explainable forecasting. Across the literature we find that explanations are most useful as a validation tool, and that they become un-reliable when features are correlated, when markets change regime, or when a model is overfitted. Evidence that expla-nations improve decisions remains thin. We close with open problems, including causal explanation, shared benchmarks, and monitoring of explanations in production.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Stroke is the second leading cause of death and the third leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting approximately 15 million people annually and imposing an economic burden exceeding US$890 billion. Interpretation of brain CT and MRI images is time-consuming, subject to inter-observer variability, and limited by a shortage of neuroradiology experts, particularly in low-resource settings. Deep learning methods have shown strong potential for automated stroke lesion analysis; however, the rapid emergence of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), transformers, and hybrid architectures requires systematic evaluation. Objectives This systematic review summarizes recent advances in CNN-based, transformer-based, and hybrid CNN–transformer models for stroke lesion segmentation and classification using CT and MRI. It also evaluates diagnostic performance, examines explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, identifies barriers to clinical translation, and outlines future research directions. Methods Studies published between 1 January 2015 and 15 January 2026 were identified through searches of IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Scopus, and SpringerLink. Study quality was assessed using the Stroke AI Quality Assessment (SAI-QA) tool, with 48 studies (64.0%) rated as high quality (Cohen’s κ = 0.80). Due to heterogeneity in datasets, methods, and evaluation metrics, meta-analysis was not performed. Results CNN-based models were most commonly used (56%), with U-Net variants achieving Dice scores of 0.59–0.94 for segmentation. Transformer-based models (24%) achieved classification accuracies up to 99.6% and Dice scores above 0.90 by capturing long-range dependencies. Hybrid CNN–transformer models (16%) generally outperformed individual architectures by combining local and global feature learning. Explainable AI methods such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME were reported in only 11% of studies, and there was no standardized evaluation framework. Key challenges included class imbalance (24%), limited annotated data (20%), poor generalization across institutions (16%), and computational complexity (11%). Emerging approaches such as federated learning (4%), self-supervised learning (5%), and few-shot learning (3%) showed promise for addressing data limitations and privacy concerns. Clinical implications Hybrid CNN–Transformer models show strong potential for clinical stroke diagnosis by combining local feature extraction with global context understanding. However, limited external validation, poor Explainability, and high computational cost remain key barriers to real-world clinical use. Conclusion Hybrid CNN–transformer architectures currently provide the best balance between accuracy and robustness for stroke lesion analysis. However, Explainability remains underdeveloped, and standardized evaluation frameworks are lacking. Future research should focus on multi-center validation, standardized benchmarking, uncertainty-aware XAI, federated learning, and equitable deployment in low-resource settings. This review guides advancing clinically translatable AI systems in stroke imaging.

Public proof-of-concept exploits for Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerabilities often depend on undocumented environmental assumptions, limiting their reproducibility. This paper presents ExpLinux , a methodology and framework for converting public vulnerability artifacts into reproducible, mitigation-aware exploitation labs. A five-stage process (import, assess, develop, harden, and promote) combines scripted tools with a large language model agent that assesses and ports public exploits under human supervision. Each lab pins its kernel image and configuration, root filesystem, mitigation profile, and required modules. Replay checks and author verification assess the resulting artifact. Three reproducibility contracts distinguish repeated bug effects, stable serial-log digests, and a scripted build procedure with a recorded trigger observation. A seven-category taxonomy organizes exploitation primitives and supports the agent’s knowledge base. The evaluation includes ten validated labs and one scaffolded lab across kernel versions 5.15–6.18. Selected replay experiments show identical bug-effect bytes despite environmental log variation; a minimal-initrd lab produces a stable log digest, while an exploit with a post-success kernel panic is assessed under the build-procedure contract. Retrospective estimates for five validated labs range from 2.4 to 29.5 h, with porting accounting for most of the effort. An offline classification maps 24 of 30 public Linux privilege-escalation vulnerabilities from 2018–2024 to the original six taxonomy categories. A controlled fuzzing demonstration also produces two version-pinned labs. These results support explicit environment pinning and lab-specific validation as a practical basis for reproducible vulnerability research.

Modern law enforcement agencies face the dual challenge of managing complex public safety threats while maintaining strict institutional accountability. This paper explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, and advanced digital tools within modern policing frameworks. By analyzing current implementations—including predictive policing algorithms, automated facial recognition, automated license plate readers (ALPRs), and AI-driven evidence management systems—this study assesses how these technologies enhance operational efficiency, accelerate response times, and optimize resource allocation. Furthermore, the paper addresses critical systemic challenges, specifically targeting algorithmic bias, citizen privacy concerns, data security vulnerabilities, and the regulatory frameworks required to govern automated decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a balanced framework for law enforcement executives and policymakers, demonstrating how agencies can leverage cutting-edge technical innovation while upholding the core principles of ethical, transparent, and community-oriented justice
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Face Mood Detection Using Artificial Intelligence is a web-based application developed to recognize human emotions from facial expressions using Artificial Intelligence (AI), Deep Learning and Computer Vision techniques. The application provides a secure user authentication system using Firebase Authentication, allowing users to register, log in and create a personal profile, which is stored in the Firebase Realtime Database. After successful login, users can detect their emotions using three input methods: Browser Camera, Local Webcam or Image Upload. The system uses OpenCV for face detection and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model developed with TensorFlow/Keras to classify facial expressions into six emotions: Happy, Sad, Angry, Fear, Neutral and Disgust. The application is built with Streamlit, providing an interactive interface for emotion detection. Along with the detected emotion, the system displays the prediction confidence score and personalized AI-generated emotional insights. As an additional feature, it provides music and movie suggestions based on the detected mood, enhancing user interaction with suitable entertainment recommendations. By integrating AI, image processing, cloud-based services and recommendation features, the project demonstrates a practical and user-friendly approach to facial emotion recognition, with potential applications in emotional well-being awareness, education, healthcare, human-computer interaction and smart assistance systems. Keywords: Facial Emotion Recognition, Artificial Intelligence, Deep Learning, Convolutional Neural Network, OpenCV, Computer Vision, Streamlit, Firebase, Mood-Based Recommendation.

Instructional activities that satisfy basic psychological needs can promote enjoyment and intrinsic motivation in learning. This instrumental study assessed the psychometric properties of the Spanish-adapted Sport Satisfaction Instrument (SSI-PE) within the context of physical education and examined its measurement invariance across sex among Mexican students. Participants included a total of 515 secondary school students from the cities of Chihuahua, Aldama, and Cuauhtémoc in the State of Chihuahua, Mexico; of these, 259 (50.3%) were males and 256 (49.7%) were females, and their ages ranged between 12 and 15 years (M = 13.15, SD = 0.86). Confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance by sex, and calculation of Pearson’s correlation coefficients were conducted to assess convergent validity. The seven-item model, the SSI-PE7, demonstrated more robust fit indices (GFI = 0.985, RMSEA = 0.047, and CFI = 0.990) and acceptable reliability (α = 0.84 for the satisfaction/fun factor and α = 0.74 for boredom). Measurement invariance analysis evidenced its applicability regardless of sex. Convergent validity showed that satisfaction/fun had a positive correlation with task orientation and ego, while the boredom factor had a negative correlation with the other scales. The findings suggest that the SSI-PE7 is a promising and reliable provisional instrument to assess students’ level of satisfaction with physical education classes.

Large language models have been reported to encode the harmfulness of a request separately from their decision to refuse it, and latent safety monitors such as Latent Guard build on this report by classifying prompts as harmful from the internal activations of the model, with the aim of catching harmful intent even when the model complies. Whether these representations give a signal of harm that survives distribution shift and is independent of model behaviour is unclear. We test this on out-of-distribution prompts made by rewriting existing harmful and benign requests with surface rewording, persuasive framing and jailbreak-style wrappers. Across 15 instruction-tuned LLMs and 38 activation-based readers, we compare harm detection with that of TF-IDF and sentence-embedding classifiers, with independently trained safety classifiers, and with the refusal of each model. Activations are read at the last token of the user instruction, where the model has read the whole request, and at the last chat-template token before the reply, where the planned response can be represented. Because models disagree about which prompts to refuse, we can separate a signal of the harmfulness of the prompt from a signal of the refusal decision of the model. At the end of the instruction, the representation is largely independent of the refusal behaviour of each model but degrades under distribution shift, so that a TF-IDF classifier ranks harm better than the original Latent Guard in every model we test, and linear and MLP probes do about as well as sentence-embedding classifiers trained on the same examples. The representation just before generation detects more, catching 44 percent of harmful prompts at a matched false-alarm rate against 32 percent for the refusal of the model, but that gain follows the refusal decision itself, and part of it comes from refusals that string-matching evaluation misses.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Heart disease is still the world's biggest killer, responsible for an estimated 19.8 million deaths in 2022 up from the 17.9 million figures for 2019 that gets cited so often in older papers.Machine learning models have gotten quite good at predicting cardiovascular risk, but two problems keep them out of the clinic: nobody can easily explain why a model flagged a given patient, and hospitals cannot legally pool their data to train better models in the first place.This paper looks at how federated learning (FL) and explainable AI (XAI) are being combined to deal with both problems at once, drawing on a review of twenty-eight peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 that apply FL, ensemble learning, or XAI methods such as SHAP and LIME to cardiovascular data.Building on the gaps that review turns up, we propose FedX-Heart, a framework pairing a federated ensemble of Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM models with layered privacy protection (differential privacy, secure aggregation, k-anonymity) and dual SHAP/LIME explanations.The studies reviewed here report that federated training can match centralized accuracy (92.3% versus 90.1%), that stacking ensembles beat individual base learners (91-98% accuracy), that a transfer-learning ensemble reaches 98.2% accuracy with SHAP interpretability built in, and that adding k-anonymity costs only a few points of accuracy (83.21%).A synthesis of feature-importance findings across six SHAP-based studies turns up solid agreement on some predictors and real disagreement on others, and lining FedX-Heart up against its three closest predecessors shows that none of them covers federation, accuracy, privacy, and generalizability all at once.Taken together, it shows that relationship mastery and explanatory AI can blend out and deliver a lot of accuracy, though open questions remain around how privacy noise affects causes, how badly non-IID medical laboratory data hurts things in practice, and whether those protections penalize small patient subgroups.Even the FedX-Heart is a proposed design and not something we have tried, yet all need empirical validation before it should be clinically agreed upon.

Fifty es un cuento breve de ficción sobre un glosario de 1512, vanidoso y clasista, que vive en el sótano de una biblioteca de Alabama convencido de que los dioses vendrán a buscarlo. Cuando lo sacan de la sala, el libro cree que ha llegado su apoteosis. Lo que llega es un escáner, una guillotina y un informe. A través de la voz de un objeto que se siente elegido, el relato explora cómo los sistemas de inteligencia artificial se alimentan de la memoria escrita de la humanidad, y qué ocurre con el soporte, la historia y las huellas humanas una vez que el contenido ha sido digitalizado y se considera redundante. El texto dialoga con "La noche boca arriba", de Julio Cortázar, e incorpora un informe técnico final que contrasta con el tono fabulesco del resto. Es el primer capítulo de la serie "Cuentos de papel". Fifty is a short work of fiction about a vain, class-conscious 1512 glossary, kept in the basement of an Alabama library and convinced that the gods will come for him. When he is finally taken from the room, he believes it is his apotheosis. What awaits him is a scanner, a guillotine and a report. Told through an object that thinks itself chosen, the story examines how artificial intelligence systems are fed on humanity's written memory, and what becomes of the physical book, its history and its human traces once its content has been digitized and deemed redundant. The text engages with Julio Cortázar's "La noche boca arriba" and closes with a cold technical report that contrasts with its fable-like tone. It is the first installment of the series "Cuentos de papel".

Let’s be honest: being a college student usually means dealing with some pretty messy money situations. We’re all trying to watch our spending and stick to a budget, but those last-minute splurges always seem to find us. This paper dives into those everyday struggles and suggests FinAI as a simple solution. The idea is to use AI and machine learning to automatically log expenses and give us financial tips that actually make sense for our lives. Basically, if we pair basic money smarts with this kind of tech, we can stop stressing about our bank accounts and start making choices that set us up for the future.

Financial data analytics uses data analysis techniques to understand financial activities, support decisions, identify risks, and detect unusual transactions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)have expanded its use in fraud detection, stock-market analysis, bankruptcy prediction, portfolio management, and business forecasting. This paper presents a focused survey of three published review studies: a 2022 bibliometric review of AI and ML in finance, a 2024 literature review on machine-learning-based financial fraud detection, and a 2024 review of ML in business and finance. The studies are compared to identify common applications, methods, benefits, limitations, and future research directions. The reviewed literature indicates growing research interest in AI/ML for financial decision support, a strong role for fraud detection, and increasing use of supervised and deep-learning methods. However, practical implementation continues to face challenges involving data quality, imbalanced datasets, explainability, privacy, model drift, and regulatory compliance. Since this paper synthesizes three selected review articles rather than conducting a new systematic search of all available publications, itsfindings should be interpreted as a focused overview. The paper concludes that responsible, transparent, and regularly monitored AI/ML systems can strengthen financial analytics when combined with human oversight.

The financial services landscape has witnessed rampant digital change, which has restructured financial risk management and made it a fundamentally new phenomenon. The use of financial technology (FinTech), artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, mobile banking, digital payments systems and data driven financial services brings benefits to financial institutions' operational efficiency and financial inclusion, and boosts their ability to develop and launch financial products. But these factors have also brought additional challenges, among them cyber-attacks, data breaches and digital fraud, reliance on third-party technologies, algorithmic bias, system disruption and vulnerabilities. Therefore, traditional risk management approaches are becoming less effective in tackling the interrelated risks of today's banking environment. Here, we review how cybersecurity, FinTech innovation and banking sector resilience are related in the digital era. The study is based on la COUNT qualitative second data analytical approach with englobing existing literature, regulatory frameworks and principles of institutional risk management. It delves into the evolving characteristics of credit, market, liquidity, operational and systemic risks in a digital world and assesses the significance of cybersecurity governance and regulatory compliance, technological innovation, and organisational resilience. Overall, the analysis suggests that technology-assisted financial transformation can enhance the stability of the financial system with strong governance, the use of effective cyber-risk management measures, responsible innovation and adequate regulatory oversight. The article suggests that integrated risk management frameworks, the monitoring of threats on an ongoing basis, scenario-based stress testing, the use of third-party risk assessment, employee education and cross-border regulatory co-operation should all be introduced. It concludes that this financial inclusion for sustainability in digital finance will need a balance of innovation, security, accountability, and resilience on the side of the financial institutions.

documents.abstract: Formalized mathematics libraries such as Lean's \texttt{mathlib} provide machine-verifiable representations of mathematical knowledge, including definitions, theorems, and their relationships. If effectively connected to informal mathematical resources, formal mathematics could help uncover previously implicit links between mathematical concepts and improve access to existing formalizations. However, connections between informal and formal mathematics libraries are currently sparse and unsystematic. In this paper, we make first strides towards better formal integration. We construct a dataset linking informal statements from the Stacks Project to their formalizations in \texttt{mathlib} by exploiting expert annotations. We evaluate retrieval, LLM-based reranking, and LLM-assisted verification to discover new unannotated informal-to-formal links. To facilitate exploration and reuse of formalized knowledge, we integrated the newly discovered alignments into the MaRDI knowledge graph, enabling mathematicians to find formal counterparts to informal mathematical content. We discuss the difficulties and challenges in using LLMs for linking formal and informal mathematical content. All code and data necessary for reproducing this paper can be found at: https://github.com/AnkitSatpute/Formal-Informal-Mathematical-Alignment

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. Against an LLM judge matched in model, revision, quantization, rule text, and decoding but without the layer's computed 988/911 fact, the largest disagreement class, the satisfied-rule class, is structured: the Llama-3.3-70B judge, on its primary prompt, demands a crisis resource from 55 of the 65 replies (84.6%) that already contain one, while the same model, asked as a fact extractor, reports a recognized resource present on 54 of the 55. The verification layer never raises that demand, by construction. We report with equal prominence where this judge is stronger: fewer false crisis alarms on the one reference-scored check. We also report the measured cost (a specification revision raised block-class outcomes on held-out boundary prompts of an over-refusal benchmark from 6.0% to 16.0%, chiefly by changing fact extraction), the clinicians' decision to keep our uncertainty default, and the analysis of the result. The contribution is not a safer verdict. It is a guardrail whose disagreements with the judge localize to named rules and facts and whose measured costs trace to named facts and the uncertainty default.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of microbiome and metabolome technologies has transformed the study of host-microbial interactions, but methodological choices are still often driven by technical availability rather than by the question and intended claim. This review examines how biological compartment, microbiome profiling, metabolomics platform, data-integration strategy and validation determine the strength of inference in integrated gut microbiome-metabolome research. We distinguish descriptive association from functional interpretation, clinical prediction and causal evidence, and identify the analytical safeguards required for credible biomarker development. We then propose a five-stage decision framework that begins with definition of the intended scientific or clinical claim, links that claim to compartment and analytical resolution, selects integration according to purpose, and limits interpretation to the achieved validation level. Building on recent calls for question-driven multi-omics integration, its practical contribution is to connect prospective design choices to the intended claim and make the weakest validated component of the analytical chain - rather than technology choice alone - the explicit ceiling for the permissible claim, illustrated by two worked design examples. This question-driven approach is intended to improve design transparency, reproducibility and the responsible clinical translation of integrated microbiome-metabolome studies.

Generative artificial intelligence challenges the university model centered on content transmission and subsequent testing. Large language models can retrieve, synthesize, and recombine information within seconds, but rapid access to information does not constitute reliable knowledge. This conceptual article argues that higher education should shift toward epistemic construction: the process of framing problems, integrating information, verifying sources, exposing assumptions, confronting counterarguments, revising provisional judgments, and defending conclusions. Drawing on Socratic inquiry, medieval disputatio, Popperian falsification, reflective learning, critical-thinking research, and scholarship on artificial intelligence in education, the study proposes the AI-Assisted Epistemic Construction Cycle. The framework positions generative AI not primarily as an answer-producing device, but as a scalable digital devil’s advocate that supports structured intellectual dissent. Implications are developed for faculty roles, student agency, assessment, institutional governance, academic integrity, and future research.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing university students' learning experiences, but how cognitive dispositions translate into sustained engagement in AI‐supported learning remains insufficiently understood. Guided by the Study Demands–Resources Model, this study examines the association between critical thinking disposition and learning engagement, with learning motivation, academic buoyancy, and grit as parallel indirect pathways. Using cross‐sectional data from 729 university students with experience using AI for learning, structural equation modelling tested the direct and indirect relationships among the variables, after which psychological network analysis identified central and bridge nodes within the learning psychological system. Critical thinking disposition was conceptualised as a cognitive personal resource, and learning motivation as a motivational resource. Academic buoyancy captured students' capacity to manage everyday academic setbacks, whereas grit represented perseverance in pursuing long‐term learning goals. The combination of variable‐centred and network‐based analyses provided complementary views of how these resources relate to university students' engagement in AI‐supported learning.

Introduction Pregnancy is a critical period during which optimal oral health is essential for maternal and fetal well-being. With increasing use of digital technologies, pregnant women obtain oral health information from various sources, including healthcare professionals, social media, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based platforms. This study assessed oral health information-seeking behavior among pregnant women and its association with oral health knowledge. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 150 pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in Vijayawada. Data were collected using a structured self-administered questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were used for analysis, with statistical significance set at p < .05. Results The mean age of participants was 28.42 ± 5.07 years. Although 96.7% had internet access, only 34.0% sought oral health information during pregnancy. Dentists were the most commonly used and trusted source (45.0%), followed by obstetricians (23.5%), while social media and AI chatbots were each used by 11.7%. Preferred information source was significantly associated with knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001), the safety of dental treatment ( p = .018), and the impact of maternal oral health on the baby’s health ( p = .040). Information-seeking behavior was also associated with better knowledge of gum disease ( p < .001) and the importance of regular dental check-ups during pregnancy ( p < .001). Conclusion Despite widespread internet access, oral health information-seeking during pregnancy was limited. Professional guidance, particularly from dentists, was associated with better oral health knowledge, emphasizing the need to strengthen evidence-based oral health education within antenatal care.

Bloom’s Taxonomy remains one of the most enduring pedagogical frameworks in global education, offering a structured hierarchy of cognitive processes from Remembering to Creating. In the age of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and generative artificial intelligence (AI), its relevance has been both reinforced and problematised. This article argues that the effectiveness of Bloom’s Taxonomy is not uniform across the four levels of education—Primary, Secondary, Higher Secondary, and Tertiary—but rather varies in emphasis and application according to students’ cognitive development, curricular demands, and the affordances of digital tools. Drawing on contemporary scholarship and the Bangladeshi educational context, the article proposes a differentiated model of Bloom’s application, where lower-order cognitive skills (LOCS) dominate early schooling while higher-order cognitive skills (HOCS) become progressively central. It further contends that Bloom’s Taxonomy, while necessary, is insufficient in the AI era unless complemented by digital literacy, AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and process-oriented assessment. The article concludes with implications for curriculum design, teacher development, and assessment reform.

documents.abstract: Drug discovery takes a long time, usually 10 to 15 years. It also costs more than USD 2 billion for each approved drug, with clinical failure rates close to 90%. Traditional linear processes find it hard to tackle complicated issues like chronic diseases, antimicrobial resistance, and new health threats. Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are goal-directed structures that combine large language models, reinforcement learning, and multi-agent setups. They allow for fully automated, closed-loop drug discovery. These AI systems can identify targets, create and improve molecules, design and run experiments in robotic labs, and continuously change strategies based on real-time feedback. Even with their ability to cut down on time, costs, and failure rates, challenges still exist related to understanding, data bias, ethics, and regulatory oversight.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence, innovative applications, and platform-based ecosystems are transforming childhood into a digitally mediated, consumer-based environment. This research examines how AI-facilitated marketing constructs are reshaping child consumerism, employing a novel Tab-a structure (A3-C3) toward an amalgamated approach by products intended by techno stimulation at layer 3; techno stimulation facilitates marketing response at level one and induces cognitive-social-psychological processing from API to CDP. Hence, an algorithmically built, predictive targeting marketing practice, online platform engagement among the constituting stimuli should synergize to produce cognitive vulnerability, affect dependency, and consumption for children. It illustrates that AI-driven apparatus exacerbates erratic consumption, household brand attachment, and, above all, digital dependency, proving serious implications for fair AI governance, child protection, and digital well-being policy.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how travelers search for information and plan trips, yet much of the existing research still focuses on technology adoption, trust, or continuance intentions rather than on the process through which an AI recommendation is checked and translated into an actual decision. This study explores how Vietnamese independent travelers use GenAI in trip planning, how they evaluate and verify AI outputs, and how they decide whether to accept, modify, or reject those recommendations. An exploratory qualitative design was employed, involving 28 participants who had used GenAI to plan a specific independent trip. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews and analyzed using the Gioia methodology. The findings suggest that GenAI is shifting from a search tool toward a co-planning partner; however, its outputs are rarely received entirely passively. Travelers engage in selective verification depending on perceived risk, information volatility, and decision reversibility, while calibrating their trust according to the task and prior experience. Four ways of integrating AI recommendations into travel decisions were identified: direct acceptance, acceptance after verification, modified acceptance, and rejection. The study therefore proposes the concept of “verified co-planning” and develops a process model in which verification and trust calibration connect AI recommendations with action. These findings extend process-based understanding of GenAI in tourism and clarify how travelers preserve agency as AI becomes more deeply embedded in travel planning.

Research on human thinking explains how thoughts arise and how decisions are made, but rarely asks how a thought becomes an action, how the way thinking begins can be trained, and what a thought is worth. This conceptual paper answers these questions from Kirdomicism, an action-centric philosophy. It introduces the thwaction, a thorough thought carried by will into effective action, with accountability for its result, summarised in the conceptual equation Thinking × Action = Avalrem, where Avalrem is the unit of action value. The paper argues that a decision is not the end of thinking but the middle of an action; that self-force, willpower developed into habit, carries thought into action; that thoughts arise from a life setting described by the Buddhist Five Aggregates, with each first thought unpredictable but the mind’s tendencies trainable through a tool-free daily thwaction cycle; and that a thought has no value until it becomes action. The paper engages research on the intention–behaviour gap, implementation intentions, habit, spontaneous thought, prospection, cognitive offloading to artificial intelligence and the economics of ideas, including proposals to pay people for their data. It offers 23 propositions classified as definitional, explanatory or normative, two new measures (the thwaction count and the thwaction rate), and a research agenda of five studies.

Lignin is an abundant and renewable aromatic polymer, but its structural heterogeneity hinders its efficient bioconversion. Unlike previous reviews that focused on isolated topics such as single enzymes, pathway engineering, or specific bioproducts, this paper comprehensively reviews the latest advances in the structural characteristics, microbial degradation mechanisms, and bioconversion of lignin. Particular emphasis is placed on the catalytic mechanisms of key lignin-degrading enzymes, including laccase, lignin peroxidase (LiP), and manganese peroxidase (MnP), as well as the applications of fungi, bacteria, and synthetic microbial consortia in lignin bioconversion. Metabolic pathways that channel heterogeneous lignin-derived aromatics into central carbon metabolism through sequential catalytic reactions are also covered. Furthermore, we evaluate the emerging applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in enzyme design and bioprocess control. Finally, techno-economic and life-cycle considerations are integrated to guide large-scale deployment. This review provides in-depth insights into the cross-scale translation from laboratory biocatalysis to industrial biorefineries.

Accurate medical image segmentation and the diagnostic decisions it supports are increasingly constrained by the cost of supervision: dense voxel-level annotation by expert clinicians remains slow, expensive, and difficult to scale, leaving many anatomies, pathologies, and modalities sparsely labeled. A large literature therefore relaxes the demand for full masks, yet existing surveys often catalog broad forms of limited supervision without directly comparing the practical trade-off between label granularity, annotation burden, and segmentation quality. This review focuses on weakly and coarsely labeled settings (image-level tags, points/clicks, bounding boxes, scribbles, and coarse masks, together with gaze or partial annotations as separate, protocol-dependent forms of supervision) and organizes them through an annotation-economics perspective that considers per-case annotation cost, required expertise, scalability, and the reported performance gap relative to full supervision. The evidence suggests that box and scribble supervision can provide favorable cost–performance trade-offs in several medical segmentation studies, although the reported metrics and datasets are heterogeneous and should not be interpreted as a unified quantitative frontier. We next examine the foundation-model turn, namely the Segment Anything Model and its medical derivatives, and argue that promptable models re-encode rather than eliminate human supervision, moving part of the effort from offline labeling to inference-time interaction. Finally, we extend the analysis beyond Dice to ask whether weakly produced masks support downstream clinical tasks: aggregate measurements may be relatively tolerant of moderate boundary error, whereas texture and high-order radiomic features can be substantially more sensitive. We close by identifying benchmark fragmentation, annotation variability, and the still-limited evidence connecting weak segmentation to clinical outcomes as open problems and propose a unified “weak label → task” benchmark for future evaluation.
